summary: Defines how IS-IS advertises link attributes on a per-application basis, so applications such as RSVP-TE, Segment Routing Policy and Loop-Free Alternates need not share one set of values. It is standards-track and was replaced by RFC 9479.

eli5.summary: Different routing jobs may want different notes about the same link. This document lets each job have its own notes in IS-IS messages. It was replaced by RFC 9479.

subtitle: Application-specific link attributes for IS-IS routing.

tldr.problem: Multiple applications (RSVP-TE, Segment Routing Policy, Loop-Free Alternates) use IS-IS link attributes for traffic engineering, but there is no way to indicate which application uses which value, or to advertise different values for the same attribute per application.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8919 defines new IS-IS advertisements: Application-Specific Link Attributes sub-TLV and Application-Specific SRLG TLV. Each includes an application identifier bit mask to tag which application(s) should use the advertised values, so different applications can have different settings on the same link.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can mix RSVP-TE, SR Policy, and LFA in the same network without confusion about which values apply to which application, and each application can have its own optimized attribute values. RFC 9479 later updated this specification.

today: RFC 8919 is a Proposed Standard. It was obsoleted by RFC 9479, which added refinements based on operational experience.

sections.title: The Problem of Multiple Applications
sections.content:
The Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) protocol is used in routers to advertise information about network links. For traffic engineering (TE), routers advertise properties of each link: its bandwidth, delay, administrative groups (colors), and other metrics. These advertised properties help routing software decide which path to use for a flow of traffic.

Historically, these link properties were used by a single application: RSVP-TE, the Resource Reservation Protocol for TE. But in recent years, other applications need the same link properties. Segment Routing Policy (SR Policy) uses them to compute explicit paths. Loop-Free Alternates (LFA) use them to choose fast backup routes. The problem is that IS-IS has no way to say which application is using each advertised value. If a router advertises a link bandwidth for SR Policy, an old RSVP-TE router might wrongly assume RSVP-TE is enabled on that link, leading to path setup failures. And different applications might want different values for the same attribute on the same link.
sections.eli5: If you ask someone for directions and they say "the road is narrow", they might mean it is too narrow for trucks but fine for cars. Different travelers care about different details. IS-IS needed a way to label which detail is for which traveler.

sections.title: Legacy Link Attributes
sections.content:
Before RFC 8919, IS-IS used sub-TLVs (Type-Length-Value sub-fields) within regular TLVs to advertise link properties. These properties include administrative group (color), maximum link bandwidth, maximum reservable bandwidth, unreserved bandwidth, TE default metric, link delay, delay variation, link loss, residual bandwidth, available bandwidth, and utilized bandwidth. These were designed for RSVP-TE and had no way to indicate which application should use them.

Additionally, IS-IS advertised Shared Risk Link Groups (SRLGs): sets of links that might fail together (for example, multiple links in the same cable bundle). SRLGs were advertised using separate TLVs for IPv4 and IPv6 links.

RFC 8919 keeps all these legacy advertisements unchanged for backward compatibility but introduces new ways to advertise the same information with application labels.
sections.eli5: Before this RFC, routers just announced link properties with no label showing who they were for. Anyone who saw the announcement would pick it up and use it.

sections.title: Application-Specific Advertisements
sections.content:
RFC 8919 introduces two new advertisement types:

1. Application-Specific Link Attributes sub-TLV (Type 16): This holds an application identifier bit mask that tags which application(s) should use the advertised link properties, followed by the property values themselves. The bit mask has two parts: a standard application bit mask (SABM) for known applications (RSVP-TE, SR Policy, LFA), and a user-defined application bit mask (UDABM) for proprietary applications. Each application gets one or more bits. For example, bit 0 identifies RSVP-TE, bit 1 identifies SR Policy, and bit 2 identifies LFA. A router can advertise an attribute with only the SR Policy bit set, making it clear that value is for SR Policy only.

2. Application-Specific SRLG TLV (Type 238): Similar to the link attributes sub-TLV, this allows application-specific SRLG advertisements. It includes link identifiers (IPv4, IPv6, or link-local/remote) and the SRLG values tagged with an application identifier bit mask. Unlike legacy SRLG TLVs, this single TLV supports all three link identifier types.

Both advertisements include an optional L-flag (legacy flag). When set, it tells receivers that the advertised application should use the legacy advertisements for that link, not these new application-specific ones.
sections.eli5: Each router can now say: "This link property is marked for Segment Routing" or "This property is for RSVP-TE". The labels are short bit flags, one bit per application.

sections.title: Deployment and Compatibility
sections.content:
RFC 8919 is designed to work alongside existing legacy advertisements, so routers can migrate gradually. The spec defines three deployment scenarios:

1. All attributes shared (common values): If RSVP-TE and SR Policy both use the same link attribute values, the network can continue using legacy advertisements for simplicity. This avoids duplication.

2. Attributes not shared: If SR Policy needs different values than RSVP-TE on some links, the router advertises the application-specific TLV with the new values, marked with the SR Policy bit. RSVP-TE continues using legacy advertisements.

3. Migration from legacy routers: Networks with old routers that do not understand application-specific TLVs must continue advertising legacy TLVs until all routers are upgraded. The migration path is: (1) send both legacy and application-specific advertisements; (2) enable application-specific processing on all routers; (3) remove legacy advertisements.

For attributes like maximum link bandwidth that are application-independent, the spec requires that all applications share one value; only the application mask differs.
sections.eli5: Old routers and new routers can work together during the switch. The network can gradually add labels to link properties without breaking anything.

sections.title: Security and Impact
sections.content:
IS-IS deployments typically run within a single administrative domain, but attackers might have access to parts of the network. IS-IS authentication mechanisms (defined in RFC 5304 and RFC 5310) protect against tampering with routing advertisements.

RFC 8919 does not introduce new security vulnerabilities because it just adds labels to existing link attribute advertisements. If an attacker tampers with an application-specific attribute, the impact is limited to that application. For example, tampering with an SR Policy attribute would affect only SR Policy routes, not RSVP-TE or LFA. However, the same authentication mechanisms that protect legacy IS-IS advertisements also protect the new application-specific ones.
sections.eli5: The security is the same as before. Routers check that messages are not forged, but now they also know which application each message is for.

left.desc: Link bandwidth = 10 Gbps. No indication of which application it is for.

right.title: Application-Specific TLV
right.desc: Link bandwidth = 10 Gbps, marked for SR Policy. Link bandwidth = 5 Gbps, marked for RSVP-TE.
